formulas: \dfrac{\textrm d}{\textrm dt}(\mathbf{f} \cdot \mathbf{g})(t) = \dfrac{\textrm d}{\textrm dt}(\mathbf{f}(t)) \cdot \mathbf{g}(t) + \mathbf{f}(t) \cdot \dfrac{\textrm d}{\textrm dt}(\mathbf{g}(t))

\begin{aligned}
\dfrac{\textrm d}{\textrm dt} (\mathbf f \cdot \mathbf g)(t)
&= \dfrac{\textrm d}{\textrm dt}(\mathbf{f}(t)) \cdot \mathbf{g}(t) + \mathbf{f}(t) \cdot \dfrac{\textrm d}{\textrm dt}(\mathbf{g}(t)) \\[3pt]
&= \left(\dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{t}} \,\mathbf i +2t \, \mathbf j \right) \cdot \left(\dfrac{1}{t} \,  \mathbf i + e^t \,  \mathbf j \right) +
\left(\sqrt{t} \,  \mathbf i + t^2 \,  \mathbf j \right) \cdot \left(-\dfrac{1}{t^2}  \, \mathbf i + e^t \, \mathbf j  \right) \\[3pt]		 
&=\dfrac{1}{2t\sqrt{t}}  +2te^t    +  \left(-\dfrac{\sqrt{t}}{t^2}\right)    + t^2e^t \\[3pt]
&=\dfrac{\sqrt{t}}{2t^2}  -  \dfrac{\sqrt{t}}{t^2} +2te^t   + t^2e^t  \\[3pt]
&= -\dfrac{\sqrt{t}}{2t^2} +\left(2t+t^2\right)e^t.
\end{aligned}

Three vectors are said to be coplanar if they are parallel to the same plane.

When we have three coplanar vectors, the parallelepiped they span is flat on the plane, and therefore its volume is zero. Consequently, the triple product of the vectors is zero as well.

So, if three vectors are coplanar, then their triple product is zero. The converse is also true: if the triple product of three nonzero vectors is zero, then the vectors are coplanar.

Intuition Behind Green's Theorem
?

There is some nice intuition behind Green's theorem that makes it easier to remember.

Suppose that is a vector field on with domain and component functions and So, we have

Green's theorem states that the sum of the microscopic curls of inside equals the macroscopic curl of at the boundary of

To keep the picture simple, we will deliberately choose to be a rectangle and imagine breaking it into many tiny squares.

Here is the key idea.

  • Each tiny square has its own local circulation, which is measured by the scalar curl If we sum (integrate) the curl at every point over the entire domain we get

  • On the other hand, when we add up the contributions from all the tiny squares, the integrals along shared interior edges cancel:

    • one square traverses a shared edge in one direction,

    • the neighboring square traverses the same edge in the opposite direction.

  • Because of this cancellation, the only edges that do not get canceled are the edges on the outer boundary

So, when we “sum all the microscopic curls” across what remains is exactly the “macroscopic curl,” meaning the circulation around the boundary:

Finally, using we can write the circulation as a line integral with respect to and

Let's now look at a concrete example of how to apply Green's theorem.

formulas: \iint\limits_D \left(\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial P}{\partial y}\right) \: \textrm{d}A  = \oint\limits_{C} P\,\mathrm{d}x + Q\,\mathrm{d}y.

The gradient of the function f(x,y,z) is defined as ∇f(x,y,z)=∂f∂xi+∂f∂yj+∂f∂zk.

Since ∇f(x,y,z)=F(x,y,z), the function f(x,y,z) must satisfy the following system: ∂f∂x=2cos⁡(2x),∂f∂y=2yz,∂f∂z=y2

First, we integrate ∂f∂x with respect to x. Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of y and z: f(x,y,z)=∫∂f∂xdx=∫2cos⁡(2x)dx=sin⁡(2x)+g(y,z)

Now, differentiating the above expression with respect to y, we obtain ∂f∂y=∂g∂y

Taking ∂f∂y=2yz into account, we obtain ∂g∂y=2yz

Now we integrate ∂g∂y with respect to y. Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of z: g(y,z)=∫∂g∂ydy=∫(2yz)dy=y2z+h(z)

Substituting g(y,z)=y2z+h(z) in the expression for f(x,y,z), we get f(x,y,z)=sin⁡(2x)+y2z+h(z).

To determine the function h(z), we differentiate f(x,y,z) with respect to z. This gives ∂f∂z=y2+h′(z).

Taking ∂f∂z=y2 into account, we obtain y2+h′(z)=y2h′(z)=0h(z)=C, where C is a constant.

Consequently, f(x,y,z)=sin⁡(2x)+y2z+C.

The work-energy principle states that the work done by a resultant force on a particle equals the change in the particle's kinetic energy. That is,

W=ΔKE

where the change in kinetic energy of a particle is given by

ΔKE=12mv12−12mv02

and m is the particle's mass, v0 is its initial velocity, and v1 is its final velocity.

The displacement of the particle is given by x(t)=2t3+t2, where t is time in seconds. We find the velocity v(t) of the particle by differentiating the displacement with respect to time:

v(t)=dxdt=ddt(2t3+t2)=6t2+2t

So, the particle's initial velocity, at t=0, is v0=v(0)=6(0)2+2(0)=0m/s, and final velocity, at t=1, is v1=v(1)=6(1)2+2(1)=8m/s.

Therefore, by the work-energy principle, the work done by the force between these times is

W=ΔKE=12⋅4⋅82−12⋅4⋅02=128−0=128J.

We differentiate using the product rule. Recall that f(x)=12ex and h(x)=−4sin⁡(x). Then,

dfdx=ddx(12ex)=12exdhdx=ddx(−4sin⁡x)=−4cos⁡(x).

Applying the product rule gives

dydx=fdhdx+hdfdx=12ex⋅(−4cos⁡(x))+(−4sin⁡(x))⋅12ex=−2ex(cos⁡(x)+sin⁡(x)).

To find the slope of the tangent line, we now substitute x=π into the formula and get

dydx|x=π=−2eπ(cos⁡(π)+sin⁡(π))=−2eπ(−1+0)=2eπ.

Therefore, the slope of the tangent line is 2eπ.

The gradient of the function f(x,y,z) is defined as ∇f(x,y,z)=∂f∂xi+∂f∂yj+∂f∂zk.

Since ∇f(x,y,z)=F(x,y,z), the function f(x,y,z) must satisfy the following system: ∂f∂x=y+1,∂f∂y=x+z+1,∂f∂z=y+1

First, we integrate ∂f∂x with respect to x. Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of y and z: f(x,y,z)=∫∂f∂xdx=∫(y+1)dx=xy+x+g(y,z)

Now, differentiating the above expression with respect to y, we obtain ∂f∂y=x+∂g∂y

Taking ∂f∂y=x+z+1 into account, we obtain

x+∂g∂y=x+z+1∂g∂y=z+1

Now, we integrate ∂g∂y with respect to y. Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of z: g(y,z)=∫∂g∂ydy=∫(z+1)dy=yz+y+h(z)

Substituting g(y,z)=yz+y+h(z) in the expression for f(x,y,z), we get f(x,y,z)=xy+x+yz+y+h(z).

To determine the function h(z), we differentiate f(x,y,z) with respect to z. This gives ∂f∂z=y+h′(z).

Taking ∂f∂z=y+1 into account, we obtain y+1=y+h′(z)h′(z)=1h(z)=z+C, where C is a constant.

Consequently, f(x,y,z)=xy+yz+x+y+z+C.
